newsitem.title: USA: Valero refining faces uphill battle after split.
newsitem.headline: Valero refining faces uphill battle after split.

text.p: Valero Energy Corp, in the midst of splitting its refining and natural gas businesses, will be faced with an ongoing battle to bolster its refining profits once the restructuring is complete, analysts say.

They said its refining business has proven to be a liability to its natural gas operations, dragging Valero's share price down and precluding stock offerings as a way to fund potential growth on either side of the business.
"Refining doesn't have any glamour in the investment community," said John Dosher of Pace Consultants in Houston.

"It's looking to us like it'll be quite a while before that changes," Dosher said, noting that relatively expensive feedstocks continue to hurt Valero's refining profits just as they do the rest of the industry.
Valero is unique in that it takes low-quality feedstocks that are cheaper than crude oil and turns them into high quality fuels. But its business suffers from poor margins.
"The refining business has been in decline since 1990 to 1991" and Valero hasn't escaped the trend, despite its special niche, said James Jordan, analyst at Williams MacKay Jordan & Co in Houston.

"There is no question we trade like a refining stock, and refining stocks trade at a discount to natural gas stocks," said Valero spokesman Keith Booke. He said Valero, as it now exists, is not likely to fuel growth attractive to investors.

But in the three weeks since Valero set plans to spin off its refining assets into a separate company and merge its natgas assets with an existing operator, its stock has traded more like a natgas stock, surging 14 percent to 28-1/2 a share, but off the $30 high hit about a week after the news.
Booke said Valero is looking at at least 24 potential suitors, and a deal could be announced as soon as February.

"Although the price of Valero stock (has gone) up more than $4 since its restructuring announcement, we think the stock has additional upside potential of at least twice that amount," said Jordan at Williams MacKay Jordan.
Jordan noted this assumes Valero will fetch a premium valuation for its natural gas assets, and that the refining side of its business will continue to drag on share price.

Under the restructuring, the refining assets look likely to continue carrying the Valero name, while the gas assets will become part of some other entity. Existing Valero shareholders will hold a stake in both entities.
Valero's Brooke said the restructuring should cut outstanding debt to around $375 million from current levels of just under $925 million, which analysts applaud.
"For Valero, if the true intent of the deal is to focus on refining and to reduce debt, then I'm cautiously optimistic," said Bruce Lanni, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co in New York.
"You're dealing with a very volatile industry and reducing debt allows greater flexibility," Lanni said.

But the trend is against Valero, with a proliferation of coking units in the Gulf lifting the price of once-cheap fuels like vacuum gas oil (VGO) and residual fuel, on which the company relies for feedstock.
The economic boom in Asia also has sucked residual and VGO across the Pacific Ocean for use in electricity generation, contributing to higher feedstock costs and bad margins.
"We have this capacity overhang and that is why margins continue to be so very bad," said Ken Miller, analyst at Houston oil consultancy Purvin & Gertz Inc.

"We see a relatively slow change," Miller added, noting improved refining profits this year for companies like Valero based on lower VGO prices may be just a blip on the screen rather than the beginning of a new trend.
-- New York Energy Desk 1 212 859 1633
